summary: Kojun Saito (1930–2002) was a scholar in Buddhist studies and Indology who studied under Seiren Matsunami. He served as a lecturer at Taisho University (attested 1965).
Kokan Fujita (b. 1944) is a Buddhist studies scholar who studied under Yujun Endo. He served as a professor at Koyasan University (attested 1995–2002).

Koken Sasaki (1931–2008) worked in Buddhist studies and Sinology. Educated at Rissho University, he later served there as assistant professor (attested 1972), department head (attested 1982–1985), professor/director (attested 2000), and professor emeritus (~2002–2008).
Koki Kawagishi (1928–2011) was a Buddhist studies scholar. In 1976, he held professorships at both Eizan Gakuin and Shitennoji University.

Komal Asrani works in computational Indology. After studying at Government Engineering College and earning a Ph.D. at Uttar Pradesh Rajarshi Tandon Open University (2002–2005), Asrani joined Babu Banarasi Das Group of Educational Institutions in 2006 in Computer Science.
Konchok Drakpa studied under Patrul Rinpoche and Jamgon Ju Mipham Gyatso. He was also a teacher of Dilgo Khyentse Rinpoche.
Konchok Gyatso is a Tibetology scholar who studied under Sherab Gyatso. He held a post at the Tibet Academy of Social Sciences (attested 2014).
Konchok Zangpo was a student of Patrul Rinpoche and Jamgon Ju Mipham Gyatso.

Konrad Gottlob Anton (1745–1814) was a scholar of linguistics and Indology. He studied at the University of Leipzig (~1763–1770) and became Professor of Oriental and Classical Languages at the University of Wittenberg in 1775.
Konrad Ihlefeld (1837–1906) was a scholar in Indology and linguistics who studied at the University of Rostock in 1858. He later served as director of Porayar Seminary from 1878 to 1885.

Konrad Klaus (b. 1956), a scholar of Indology and Tibetology, studied at Göttingen and Marburg under Wilhelm Rau and Michael Hahn. He held visiting professorships at Bochum, Marburg, and Bonn (1999–2001) before succeeding Claus Vogel in 2001.
Konrad Meisig (b. 1953) is an Indology and Buddhist studies scholar who studied under Ulrich Schneider (~1978–1985). He served at Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz from circa 1990 to 2019.

Kosaku Hamada (1881–1938) was a scholar of archaeology, history, Sinology, and Japanology. After studying at the University of Tokyo (~1901–1904), he held posts at the University of Tokyo (~1905–1909) and Kyoto University (~1909–1938).

Kosei Ishii (b. 1950) specializes in Buddhist studies and philosophy. He studied at Waseda University under Akira Hirakawa, and later held posts at Waseda, Komazawa Junior College (1994–2006), and Komazawa University (2006–2021).

Kosei Tada (1938–2017) was a Buddhist studies scholar who studied at the University of Tokyo. He held positions at Taisho University (~1994–2009) and served as board chairman of the Society for Buddhist Cultural Studies (attested 2004).
Koshin Suzuki (b. 1959) is a scholar in Buddhist studies and Indology. He completed doctoral studies at Taisho University and held a researcher post there (attested 1995–1998).

Koshiro Tamaki (1915–1999) worked in Buddhist studies, Indology, and philosophy. Educated at the Fifth Higher School and the University of Tokyo, he held professorships at the University of Tokyo (1964–1976), Tohoku University (~1976–1979), and Nihon University (1979–1986).

Kosho Kawamura (b. 1924) studied Indology and Buddhist studies at Toyo University under teachers including Giyu Nishi and Nichijin Sakamoto. He held posts at Toyo University, Minobusan University (attested 1996), and Nava Nalanda Mahavihara (attested 2001).

Kosho Mizutani (1928–2014) was a Buddhist studies scholar educated at Ryukoku and Bukkyo universities. He served at Bukkyo University as assistant professor (~1959–1975) and president (~1975–1989), and headed Bukkyo Kyoiku Gakuen and Tokai Gakuen.

Kosho Uchiyama (1912–1998) was a Buddhist studies and philosophy scholar who studied at Waseda and under Kodo Sawaki. He taught at Miyazaki Catholic Seminary (~1937–1941) and later succeeded Sawaki as abbot of Antai-ji (1965–1975).
